ΤΗΣ ΕΥΡΕΣΕΩΣ ΤΟΥ ΤΙΜΙΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΖΩΟΠΟΙΟΥ ΣΤΑΥΡΟΥ.
4077Κατ' ἐκεῖνον τὸν χρόνον ὁ τῆς Αἰλίας ἐπίσκοποςΜακάριος ὁ φερώνυμος
ἦν Ἑρμονᾶν διαδεξάμενος. Ὁ δὲ Μέγας Κωνσταντῖνος μονοκράτωρ γενόμενος
πᾶσαν τὴν φροντίδα εἰς τὰ θεῖα μετήνεγκεν. Ἀνοικο ομῶν τὰς ἐκκλησίας, ἐπεὶ
φιλοτίμως πλουτῶν [ἦν] ἐκ τοῦ δημοσίου λόγου, ἔν τε χρήμασι καὶ ἀναλώμασι, καὶ
παντοίοις κειμηλίοις. Καὶ πρῶτον νόμον ἔγρα ψεν ἀποδίδοσθαι τοὺς τῶν εἰδώλων
ναοὺς τοῖς τῷΧριστῷ ἀφιερωμένοις, καὶ τοὺς ἕτι εἰδωλολατροῦν τας, κεφαλικαῖς
ἐπιτιμᾶσθαι τιμωρίαις. ∆εύτερον νόμον ἔγραψεν, Χριστιανοὺς μόνους
ὀρθοδοξοῦντας στρατεύεσθαι, ἐθνῶν τε καὶ στρατοπέδων τούτους ἄρχειν. Τρίτον
νόμον ἔγραψεν, ἀπράκτους εἶναι τὰς πασχαλίας ἑβδομάδας δύο, μίαν πρὸ, καὶ μίαν
μετά. Καὶ ἦν λοιπὸν εἰρήνη βαθεῖα, καὶ χαρὰ ἐν ὅλῃ τῇ οἰκουμένῃ, πάντων τῶν
ἐθνῶν ὁσημέραι προστρε χόντων τῇ πίστει, καὶ βαπτιζομένων, καὶ ἰδίαις χερσὶ τοὺς
πατρῴους θεοὺς συντριβόντων.Ἀλλὰ ταῦτα οὐκ ἦν φορητὰ τῷ ἀλάστορι δαίμονι,
ἀλλὰ πάλιν εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἐδραματούργει, πῶς ἂν ἐκκό ψει τὴν τοσαύτην τῶν
ἀνθρώπων χαρμονήν. Καὶ πεῖσαι μὲν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους θεοποιεῖσθαι τὴν κτίσιν
οὐκέτι οἷός τε ἦν· ἐφωράθη γὰρ ἡ ἀπάτη αὐτοῦ. Τὸν δὲ Κτίστην συντάξαι τοῖς
κτίσμασι παραπεῖσαι ἐπει ράθη τοὺς ἀστηρίκτους. Καὶ ἦν πάλιν τάραχος οὐκ ὀλίγος
ἐν ταῖς Ἐκκλησίαις τοῦ Θεοῦ, Ἀρείου τινὸς Ἀλεξανδρέως ἄνω καὶ κάτω κυκλοῦντος,
καὶ τὴν οἰκουμένην ταράττοντος. Συναπήχθησαν δὲ αὐτῷ ἐπίσκοποί τινες ὀλίγοι τὸν
ἀριθμὸν, ὧν πρῶτος Εὐ σέβιος ὁ Νικομηδείας, καὶ Εὐσέβιος ὁ Παμφίλου, καὶ ἕτεροι
σὺν αὐτοῖς. Θεωρῶν δὲ τὴν μεγάλην φιλο νεικίαν ὁ Μέγας Κωνσταντῖνος, ἠνιᾶτο
τὴν ψυχήν· καὶ πρῶτον μὲν ἐπειρᾶτο διὰ παραινετικῶν γραμμά των τῶν ἑκατέρων
μερῶν κατασβέσαι τὴν ἔριν. Ὡς δὲ ἴδεν ἀνήκεστον γινόμενον τὸ κακὸν, προσέταξε
γενέσθαι οἰκουμενικὴν σύνοδον ἐν τῇ Νικαέων πόλει, καὶ συνῆλθον ἐπίσκοποι τὸν
ἀριθμὸν τριακόσιοι δέκα καὶ ὀκτώ. Ὧν οἱ πλεῖστοι ἦσαν ὁμολογηταὶ, τὰ στί γματα
τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐν τῷ σώματι βαστάζοντες. Ἦν δὲ σὺν αὐτοῖς καὶ ὁ πανεύφημος
Κωνσταντῖνος, καὶ δὴ τῆς ὑποθέσεως κινηθείσης, ἔκθεσιν πίστεως ἔγ γραφον
ἐξήνεγκαν, τὴν κατὰ πᾶσαν Ἐκκλησίαν ὀρθοδόξων νῦν ἀπαγγελλομένην. Τοὺς δὲ
περὶ Ἄρειον καὶ Εὐσέβιον τὸν Νικομηδέα ἐπιμένοντας τῇ κακοδοξίᾳ ἀνεκήρυξαν,
καὶ ἐξωρίσθησαν, καὶ ἐχειροτονήθησαν ἕτεροι ἀντ' αὐτῶν. Φιλοτιμησάμενος δὲ ὁ
βασιλεὺς τοὺς ἐπισκόπους, καὶ ἀσπασάμενος ἀπέλυσε μετ' εἰρήνης εἰς τὰς ἰδίας
παροικίας, χαί ρων ἐπὶ τῇ συμφωνίᾳ τῶν Ἐκκλησιῶν.Παρεκελεύσατο δὲ τῷ τῆς
Αἰλίας ἐπισκόπῳ Μα καρίῳ παρόντι ἐν τῇ συνόδῳ, καὶ τῶν ἀποστολικῶν δογμάτων
ὑπερμαχοῦντι ἀναζητῆσαι τὸν ζωοποιὸν σταυρόν, καὶ τὸ θεοδόχον μνῆμα, καὶ
πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους τόπους, καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους δὲ ἐπισκόπους ὁμοίως 4080
προετρέψατο, αἰτήσασθαι, εἴ τι συνορᾷ εἰς ἀπαρτι σμὸν ἔκαστος τῆς ἰδίας Ἐκκλησίας.
Ἦν δὲ ἐννεακαιδέκατον ἔτος τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ, ὅτε ἐγένετο κατὰ Νίκαιαν
σύνοδος.Μετὰ ταῦτα ἀπέστειλεν ὁ βασιλεὺς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ μητέρα Ἑλένην, τὴν
ἀξιέπαινον καὶ θεοφιλῆ, εἰς Ἱεροσόλυμα, μετὰ γραμμάτων καὶ χρημάτων ἀφθονίας,
πρὸς τὸν φερώνυμον Μακάριον τῆς Αἰλίας ἐπίσκοπον ἐπὶ ἀναζητήσει τοῦ ζωοποιοῦ
ξύλου τοῦ ἐνδόξου σταυροῦ καὶ οἰκοδομῇ τῶν ἁγίων τόπων· αὐτῆς τοῦτο αἰτησάσης
τῆς βασιλίδος, φασκούσης ὀπτασίαν τινὰ θείαν ἑωρακέναι κελεύουσαν αὐτῇ τὰ
Ἱεροσόλυμα καταλαβεῖν, καὶ τοὺς ἁγίους τόπους εἰς φῶς ἀγαγεῖν χωσθέντας ὑπὸ

thought_title: Constantine's laws, Nicaea, and Helena's mission
orientation: The narrator opens the encomium by setting the scene under Bishop Macarius of Aelia and Emperor Constantine, whose laws establish Christian peace until Arius disturbs the churches, leading to the Council of Nicaea and Helena's journey to Jerusalem.
pass_a_gloss: At that time the bishop of Aelia, Macarius (meaning "blessed"), had succeeded Hermonas. And the Great Constantine, having become sole ruler, transferred all his care to divine things. He was rebuilding the churches, since he was generously wealthy from the public treasury, both in money and in expenditures and in all kinds of treasures. And first he wrote a law that the temples of the idols be given over to those consecrated to Christ, and that those still practicing idolatry be punished with capital punishments. Second he wrote a law that only orthodox Christians serve as soldiers, and that these rule over nations and armies. Third he wrote a law that the two Paschal weeks be free from work, one before and one after. And there was henceforth deep peace and joy in the whole inhabited world, as all the nations daily came over to the faith and were baptized and with their own hands shattered their ancestral gods. But these things were not bearable to the avenging demon, but again he plotted within himself how he might cut out so great a joy of humans. And to persuade humans to make the creation divine he was no longer able; for his deceit had been detected. But to persuade the unstable to rank the Creator with the creatures he attempted. And there was again no small disturbance in the churches of God, as a certain Arius of Alexandria circulated up and down and troubled the inhabited world. And some few bishops in number were carried away with him, of whom first was Eusebius of Nicomedia, and Eusebius of Caesarea, also called Pamphili, and others with them. And seeing the great contentiousness, the Great Constantine was grieved in his soul; and first he tried through advisory letters of both parties to quench the strife. But when he saw the evil becoming incurable, he commanded that an ecumenical council be held in the city of the Nicaeans, and bishops came together in number three hundred and eighteen. Of whom the majority were confessors, bearing the marks of Jesus in their body. And with them was also the all-praised Constantine, and when the matter was set in motion, they produced a written statement of faith, the one now proclaimed throughout every church of the orthodox. And those around Arius and Eusebius of Nicomedia who persisted in evil doctrine they denounced, and they were exiled, and others were ordained in their place. And having honored the bishops generously and embraced them, the emperor sent them away with peace to their own districts, rejoicing at the harmony of the churches. And he urged Macarius, the bishop of Aelia, who was present at the council and fighting on behalf of the apostolic doctrines, to search for the life-giving Cross and the holy tomb that received God and all the holy places, and he likewise encouraged the other bishops to ask for whatever each saw fit for the completion of his own church. And it was the nineteenth year of his reign when the council at Nicaea took place. After these things the emperor sent his own mother Helena, the praiseworthy and beloved by God, to Jerusalem, with letters and an abundance of money, to Macarius (meaning "blessed"), bishop of Aelia, for the search for the life-giving wood of the glorious Cross and the building of the holy places; the queen herself having requested this, claiming to have seen a certain divine vision commanding her to reach Jerusalem and to bring to light the holy places that had been buried by the winds and had become invisible for so many years. And the bishop, having learned that the queen had arrived, gathered the bishops of the province and met her with fitting honor.

choices.why: The epithet puns on Macarius's name meaning 'blessed'; 'aptly named' preserves the wordplay without adding a gloss.
ἀλάστωρ is a specific Greek term for an avenging spirit; 'avenging demon' keeps the demonic sense and the epithet.
Literal rendering of the compound; 'God-receiving' preserves the active sense of δέχομαι.

choices.term: ἀπράκτους εἶναι τὰς πασχαλίας ἑβδομάδας δύο
choices.english: that the two Paschal weeks be free from work
choices.why: ἄπρακτος means 'without business/work'; 'free from work' is literal and clear for a legal provision.

choices.term: τὰ στίγματα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐν τῷ σώματι βαστάζοντες
choices.english: bearing the marks of Jesus in their body
choices.why: Echoes Galatians 6:17; 'marks' is the standard rendering of στίγματα, and 'bearing' keeps βαστάζω.
θεοφιλής is a passive compound 'loved by God'; the glossary bans hyphenated compounds, so a phrasal rendering is used.

bible_refs.note: τὰ στίγματα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐν τῷ σώματι βαστάζοντες

pass_b_english: At that time the bishop of Jerusalem was Macarius (meaning "blessed"), who had succeeded Hermonas. When Constantine the Great became sole ruler, he turned all his attention to divine things. He rebuilt the churches, since he was generous with the public treasury, with public funds and all kinds of resources. And first he wrote a law that the temples of the idols be handed over to those consecrated to Christ, and that those who still practiced idolatry be punished with severe penalties. Second, he wrote a law that orthodox Christians should serve in the army, and that these should command both nations and camps. Third, he wrote a law that the two Paschal weeks be free from work, one before and one after. And from then on there was deep peace and joy in the whole world, as all the nations daily came running to the faith, and were baptized, and with their own hands shattered their ancestral gods.

But these things were not bearable to the avenging demon, and he plotted how he might destroy such great joy among human beings. The demon was no longer able to persuade people to make a god of creation, for his deception had been exposed. But he attempted to persuade the unstable to rank the Creator with created things. And again there was no small disturbance in the churches of God, as a certain Arius of Alexandria went about everywhere, throwing the world into confusion. A few bishops, small in number, were carried away with him, of whom the first was Eusebius of Nicomedia, and Eusebius of Caesarea, also called Pamphili, and others with them. When Constantine the Great saw the great strife, he was grieved in his soul. At first he tried through letters of exhortation to extinguish the quarrel between the two parties. But when he saw that the evil was becoming incurable, he ordered an ecumenical council to be held in the city of Nicaea, and three hundred eighteen bishops assembled. Most of them were confessors, bearing the marks of Jesus in their body (Galatians 6:17). With them also was the most renowned Constantine, and when the matter was set in motion, they produced a written statement of faith, the one now proclaimed in every orthodox church, declaring the Son one in being with the Father. Those around Arius and Eusebius of Nicomedia who persisted in their false teaching they denounced, and they were exiled, and others were ordained in their place. The emperor honored the bishops, embraced them, and sent them away in peace to their own dioceses, rejoicing at the harmony of the churches.

He instructed Macarius, the bishop of Jerusalem, who was present at the council and fighting for the apostolic doctrines, to search for the life-giving Cross, and the holy tomb that received God, and all the holy places. He likewise urged the other bishops to ask for whatever each saw fit for the completion of his own church. It was the nineteenth year of his reign when the council at Nicaea took place.

After these things the emperor sent his own mother Helena, praiseworthy and beloved by God, to Jerusalem, with letters and an abundance of money, to Macarius (meaning "blessed"), bishop of Jerusalem, for the search for the life-giving wood of the glorious Cross and the building of the holy places. The queen herself had asked for this, saying that she had seen a divine vision commanding her to go to Jerusalem and bring to light the holy places that had been buried by the winds and had been hidden for so many years. When the bishop learned that the queen had arrived, he gathered the bishops of the province and met her with fitting honor.

last_rejected.why: The brief maps 'Εὐσέβιος ὁ Παμφίλου' to 'Eusebius of Caesarea' with note 'traditionally called Eusebius Pamphili (Eusebius, son of Pamphilus), the church historian.' The glossary/brief specifies the modern name mapping. Using 'Pamphili' without 'of Caesarea' breaks the name mapping.
last_rejected.ruling: Εὐσέβιος ὁ Παμφίλου literally means 'Eusebius son of Pamphilus'; 'Eusebius Pamphili' is a standard rendering, not a glossary-breaking error.

last_rejected.quote: The queen herself had asked for this, saying that she had seen a divine vision
last_rejected.source_quote: αὐτῆς τοῦτο αἰτησάσης τῆς βασιλίδος, φασκούσης ὀπτασίαν τινὰ θείαν ἑωρακέναι
last_rejected.why: The brief states Helena's motivation is marked by participial clause (αὐτῆς... αἰτησάσης and φασκούσης) describing her request and claim, 'not direct or indirect quoted speech.' The English 'saying that she had seen' with 'that' clause makes this indirect quoted speech, misrepresenting the grammatical voice marking.
last_rejected.fix: The queen herself having asked for this, claiming to have seen a divine vision
last_rejected.ruling: φασκούσης ἑωρακέναι is naturally rendered 'saying that she had seen'; participial claim becomes indirect speech in English without misleading the reader.

last_rejected.why: ἀνέμων here means not 'winds' but likely 'enemies/demons' or is a textual variant/corruption for ἀνθρώπων or similar; 'winds' burying places makes no sense. The context demands enemies or persecutors buried/hid the holy places.
last_rejected.ruling: χωσθέντας ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνέμων literally means 'buried by the winds'; the translator renders the source text accurately and should not silently emend.

problems.fix: Use 'Eusebius of Caesarea (called Pamphili)' consistently.

problems.fix: Note in introduction that these are all epithets for same Cross.

problems.fix: Emend to 'generous with the public treasury...'

The name clarification is handled by the edit adding 'of Caesarea'.
The name meaning 'aptly named' is already used only once for Macarius in this excerpt.

fixed: The varied epithets for the Cross (life-giving, glorious, precious) all refer to the same Cross of Christ; the source uses multiple epithets, and the English preserves them faithfully.

The English already renders the Nicene faith statement without using a different term for homoousios; the phrase 'one now proclaimed in every orthodox church' does not introduce a conflicting rendering, but an explanatory clause has been added to clarify the creedal term.
